2
What is the effect of a systematic error on the measurement of a physical quantity?
A
It limits the precision of the measured value.
B
It limits the range of values obtained in repeated measurements.
C
It results in repeated measurements having different values from each other.
D
It results in the measured value being different from the correct value.

hints: Notice the phrase systematic error in the stem and contrast it with random error that causes scatter in repeated measurements.
Connect precision to agreement between repeats and accuracy to agreement with the correct value, then ask which one a constant bias affects.
Picture a zero error such as an uncalibrated balance that adds the same offset to every reading and consider what happens to the mean value.
walkthrough: Identify the key term: systematic error means a consistent bias present in the measuring system, such as zero error or faulty calibration.
State the rule: random errors cause spread about a mean and affect precision, while systematic errors shift the mean away from the true value and affect accuracy.
Apply to repeats: because the bias is the same each time, repeated measurements stay closely grouped and do not show different values from each other.
Conclude that the grouped mean is displaced from the correct value, so the measured value differs from the correct value. This is option D.

A.explanation: Precision describes spread of repeated readings. Random errors limit precision, not systematic errors.

B.explanation: The range of repeated values is set by random variation. A systematic error shifts all readings the same way.

C.explanation: Different values on repeats show random error. A systematic error repeats consistently in the same direction.

D.explanation: A systematic error biases every reading away from the true value, so accuracy is lost even if repeats agree.
